title: QED’s Victoria Zuo Flags Trust Gap in Agentic Payments
snippet: QED Investors partner Victoria Zuo says AI agents handling financial transactions need a risk premium model akin to card-present versus card-not-present interchange. The post QED’s Victoria Zuo Flags Trust Gap in Agentic Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A senior investor at QED Investors has outlined a framework for thinking about risk and trust in agentic payments, arguing that the financial industry has yet to price the new liability surface that autonomous AI agents create when they transact on behalf of consumers.

Victoria Zuo, partner at QED Investors

Victoria Zuo, a San Francisco-based partner at the venture firm, said the clearest analogy already exists inside the payments infrastructure: the long-established difference in interchange rates between card-present and card-not-present transactions, which reflects the higher fraud risk of a transaction completed without a physical card and a human at the terminal.

“Vendors should be properly rewarded for that risk, similar to how interchange fees are different between card-present and card-not-present transactions,” Zuo said, describing a category she labels human-present and human-not-present transactions. Authentication and authorisation, she added, are the key controls for limiting chargebacks and fraudulent requests in an agentic environment.

The trust gap

Zuo said the gap between the technology’s capability and institutional trust in it remains wide, and that she herself reflects the ambivalence many professionals feel. Despite being an active follower of AI developments, she has not connected her bank accounts to a general-purpose AI assistant.

“It comes down to trust. I still haven’t linked my bank accounts to my ChatGPT Pro account,” she said, adding that she expects specialist vertical agents in financial services and healthcare to earn that trust before general-purpose horizontal agents do.

Her investment interest follows from that view. She said startups focused on granular permission controls for payments, the kind of architecture that would let a user instruct an agent to transact only within defined parameters, represent a category worth watching.

Agents as a new distribution channel

A second thread in Zuo’s analysis concerns how merchants and financial-services providers need to rethink distribution when the end customer is an AI agent rather than a person. She pointed to Lorikeet, a Sydney-based portfolio company, as an example of a startup already building infrastructure on this assumption. The company recently launched a product designed to help merchants serve structured information, including product descriptions, return policies and refund terms, directly to agents completing transactions on behalf of consumers.

“Now that transactions are happening with consumers closing the purchasing loop, you want to serve up the information packet including product descriptions, return policies and refund policies to the agent rather than humans,” Zuo said.

The observation points to a broader shift in how conversion funnels are being redrawn. As AI agents increasingly handle discovery, comparison and purchase completion, the optimisation task for merchants moves from search-engine ranking and click-through rates toward making data legible to machine decision-makers.

Market context

The trust and liability questions Zuo raises sit at the centre of a fast-developing regulatory debate. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority has yet to publish formal guidance on accountability when an AI agent causes or fails to prevent a financial loss, though its Consumer Duty framework requires firms to demonstrate good outcomes for clients regardless of which layer of the stack interacts with them. In the EU, the AI Act’s tiered risk classification and PSD3’s strong customer authentication requirements both bear on agentic payment scenarios, though the interplay between the two frameworks remains unsettled.

From an investment standpoint, QED’s framing, that financial services could function as a revenue model embedded inside personal AI agents rather than as a standalone product category, suggests the firm is looking beyond pure-play fintech into the infrastructure that routes and controls money inside AI-native applications. The near-term signal will be which startups secure the first credible licensing arrangements or banking-as-a-service partnerships to underpin those capabilities.

title: FinTech Wales Meets Economy Minister on Capital, Talent and Growth
snippet: Industry leaders and Cabinet Minister Adam Price discussed funding access, skills gaps and how Welsh fintechs can scale internationally. The post FinTech Wales Meets Economy Minister on Capital, Talent and Growth appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
FinTech Wales convened a roundtable with Adam Price MS, Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, on 1 October, bringing together leaders from across Wales’ fintech and financial services sector to address three structural constraints: access to capital, talent pipelines and international growth.

Companies represented at the event, hosted at Tŷ Admiral in Cardiff, included Admiral, Hodge Bank, Principality, Vodafone Business, Collections Cloud, IE Hub, Driverly and several other Welsh fintech and financial services firms. The session was framed as a direct exchange between industry and government, rather than a formal consultation, with the intent of surfacing actionable commitments.

Capital and culture

A recurring theme was Wales’ risk-averse investment culture, which several attendees said was limiting the ambition of early-stage companies. One participant called for a regulatory or policy sandbox that would give companies room to develop genuinely innovative products without facing disproportionate commercial risk during development. Another drew a comparison with Silicon Valley’s tolerance for failure, arguing that Wales needs a similar cultural shift if it is to compete for capital on a global stage.

The cost pressures on smaller businesses were also raised directly, with corporation tax, national insurance and PAYE obligations cited as disincentives to growth. Attendees argued that fiscal incentives need to be rebalanced to make Wales a more competitive destination for founders and investors alike.

Skills and specialisation

On talent, the group’s clearest message was that the skills system in Wales should be employer-led rather than supply-driven. Several specific skills shortages were identified as part of an informal audit conducted during the discussion, though these were not published in detail. Attendees also cautioned against pursuing broad technology trends without first identifying the subsegments where Wales has a genuine comparative advantage, pointing to Admiral’s development of specialist insurance expertise as the model to follow.

Sarah Jones, chief executive of FinTech Wales, said the session produced clear actions: “One of the clearest messages from around the table was the need to create easier access to funding and remove some of the red tape that prevents companies being able to move swiftly in their respective markets.”

The minister closed the discussion by acknowledging Wales’ productivity gap relative to the rest of the UK and stressing the role of the recently established Welsh development agency in co-ordinating industry input. He committed the Welsh Government to continued engagement with the sector and to promoting Welsh fintech strengths internationally.

Broader context

Wales occupies a relatively modest position in the UK’s regional fintech landscape. While clusters in Cardiff have grown since FinTech Wales launched in 2019, the region competes with better-capitalised hubs in London, Edinburgh, Manchester and Leeds for both talent and venture funding. The UK government’s own regional investment policies, including Levelling Up commitments, have delivered mixed outcomes for financial services outside London, and Welsh Government devolved economic levers are limited compared with those available to the Scottish Government, which has its own fintech strategy and dedicated public funding vehicles.

The conversation at the FinTech Wales roundtable reflects a pattern visible across smaller regional ecosystems: structural barriers to capital and skills are well understood, but translating political engagement into concrete funding mechanisms or regulatory accommodations remains the harder step. The reference to a development agency open to industry input is worth monitoring, as is any follow-through on the sandbox proposal, which would require co-ordination with the FCA’s existing innovation pathways.

FinTech Wales has more than 200 members and operates as a not-for-profit body. Further details on its events programme are available at fintechwales.org.

title: FXB Summit 2026: why cross-border payments need partners
snippet: Instant payments, stablecoins and inclusion led the fourth FXB Summit in Dubai, where speakers agreed collaboration matters as much as the technology itself. The post FXB Summit 2026: why cross-border payments need partners appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The future of cross-border payments will depend as much on how financial institutions work together as on the technology they deploy. That was the message running through the fourth Future Cross Border (FXB) Payments Summit, held at the Anantara Downtown Dubai

The summit, founded by Shafique R Ibrahim and run by the events platform Fintership, brought banks, exchange houses, fintechs, payment providers and regulators together for a single day of panels and keynotes. Its supporting partners included the UAE Banks Federation, the Foreign Exchange and Remittance Group (FERG), Al Etihad Payments and Swift. The Fintech Times’ events correspondent Phil Smith was in attendance, and this summary draws on his notes from the day.

The agenda ranged across instant payments, artificial intelligence, digital assets, compliance and financial inclusion. In most sessions, the question was less whether the technology works and more how institutions, jurisdictions and regulators join it up.

A regulator that co-authors innovation

Adeeb Ahamed, Managing Director of LuLu Financial Holdings, credited the UAE’s supportive regulatory environment and its ability to attract international talent for the country’s rise as a financial innovation hub.

“The regulator has been a co-author for innovation here,” he said, pointing to the willingness of UAE authorities to back new business models.

His view of what comes next centred on partnership rather than building everything in-house. “I’m a great believer of partnerships. I believe that the future lies in partnerships,” he said. “Build what is necessary, and then find partners who can help you scale.”

On artificial intelligence, Ahamed described a human-in-the-loop approach at LuLu Financial Holdings. AI is being used to make areas such as compliance and auditing more efficient, while people retain oversight and customers keep control over their own financial decisions.

Taking instant payments across borders

Domestic instant payments have moved quickly in the UAE, where Al Etihad Payments operates the Aani instant payments platform. Carrying that speed across borders is a harder problem, and it was the focus of a panel with Andrea Cianchetti, Chief Product Officer at Al Etihad Payments, Roberto Mancone, CEO of du Pay, and Omer Farooq, CEO of Blue Remit.

Once a payment leaves the country, it meets foreign exchange conversion, settlement, differing regulatory requirements and the challenge of making separate systems interoperate. The panel’s view was that the domestic progress is real, but the international leg still carries most of the friction.

A separate session, Who Owns the Cross-Border Experience?, moderated by Muhammad Waqar Ashraf of Swift, asked who is accountable when a payment passes through several hands.

“The real challenge is moving value across institutions, jurisdictions and, of course, currencies,” said Nawal Kebouri Ammor, Group Head of Financial Institutions at Al Ansari Financial Services. She pointed to the differing settlement arrangements, liquidity requirements and regulatory frameworks that continue to complicate cross-border transactions.

Panellists also stressed that the experience of the person receiving a payment matters as much as that of the sender, particularly when the money moves through several financial institutions before it arrives.

Digital assets over the next 24 months

The practical use of digital assets was another focus, with speakers from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), RAKBANK, the Dubai Digital Asset Association and Fuze looking at what the next two years are likely to bring.

Stablecoins and tokenised money offer an alternative route for international settlement and money transfers. The panel was clear, however, that wider adoption will depend on regulatory clarity, liquidity and compatibility with the financial infrastructure banks already run. Speakers returned several times to the need for regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to work together as digital assets move into mainstream financial services, a point with particular weight in a city that set up a dedicated virtual assets regulator in 2022.

Financial inclusion beyond access

Syed Muhammad Ali, CEO of myZoi Financial Inclusion Technologies, focused on the lower-income workers who still rely heavily on cash, despite near-universal smartphone ownership in the UAE.

When myZoi began operating, more than 90 per cent of the salaries paid into its accounts were withdrawn in cash. Two years later, that figure had fallen below 50 per cent.

“The margin for error is non-existent,” Ali said. Many of these workers send a substantial share of their earnings home, so a single failed or delayed transfer can do lasting damage to trust. For this group, reliability is what drives digital adoption, not access alone.

Collaboration and competition

The summit also examined how the relationship between traditional institutions and technology-led providers is changing. Hasan Fardan Al Fardan, CEO of Al Fardan Exchange, took part in a leadership discussion on the roles each will play in cross-border payments, a theme he had set out ahead of the event: that progress depends on linking innovation with interoperability, governance and trust.

That framing carried through the wider discussion, as banks, exchange houses and fintechs described adapting to a payments landscape in which no single institution controls the full journey of a transaction.

By the close, the consistent challenge was turning technological progress into measurable improvements for consumers and businesses: international payments that are faster, cheaper, more transparent and more dependable. Those are the same four measures in the G20 roadmap for enhancing cross-border payments, coordinated by the Financial Stability Board, which sets its targets for cost, speed, transparency and access to be met by the end of 2027.

title: Ramp seeks bank charter
snippet: Ramp's applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust bank charter on Friday.
fullText:
Corporate spend management fintech Ramp applied for a national trust bank charter Friday with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the company wrote Monday in posts on X and LinkedIn.

The company offered few details, saying it would offer fiduciary investment management and digital-asset custody – but would not take deposits or make commercial loans – if the charter is approved. 

“The proposed trust bank would bring these services under a consistent federal regulatory framework, helping us build great products alongside our banking partners to further our mission to save businesses time and money,” the company wrote in its posts.

There has been a competitive rush for charters this year. Block, Avant and Modern Treasury are among the fintechs that have sought OCC charters, all applying over the past two months. They're eager to have access to the Federal Reserve's account and payment rail services.

Ramp’s application was filed just a day after the company announced it had raised $1.85 billion in a financing round led by Dragoneer Investment Group. Ramp is now valued at $60 billion.

The application also comes just weeks after the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing the recent spike in national trust bank charter applications – and approvals – are creating “a gaping hole in financial regulation.” 

The OCC’s current posture “perversely allow[s] entities engaged in highly risky cryptocurrency and digital assets activities to enter the banking system under lightly regulated national charters rather than the more rigorously regulated traditional bank charter,” which puts community banks at a “severe competitive disadvantage,” the trade group asserted in its lawsuit, filed Oct. 2.

The OCC has approved, or conditionally approved, 21 national trust bank charters since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the ICBA noted. Thirteen of those have come from crypto companies, the trade group said.

“There is no statutory basis for the OCC’s position that it can charter crypto trust banks that are neither depository nor fiduciary,” the ICBA argued in its lawsuit.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould, however, has defended his agency’s conditional charter approvals, saying “we don’t have a zero risk tolerance anymore.”

“That’s not what the statute says. The statute talks about a reasonable chance of success. That’s how we evaluate applications,” Gould said at an event in May. 

Ji Hun Kim, CEO of trade association Crypto Council for Innovation, said ICBA’s lawsuit “is a clear attempt to resist national trust charters, payments innovation, and competition in financial services.”

“Restricting banking to legacy business models will not stop demand for financial innovation,” Kim said this month. 

Ramp, for its part, has solidified its leadership this year, naming co-founder Karim Atiyeh, previously the company’s chief technology officer, as co-CEO, alongside co-founder Eric Glyman.

Additionally, Ramp tapped Rahul Sengottuvelu, previously its head of applied artificial intelligence, to become its next tech chief. Before joining Ramp, Sengottuvelu served as CTO at Cohere, which Ramp bought in 2023.

title: Latvia Issues 20-Plus Fintech Licences in 2026 as EU Gateway Push Grows
snippet: Latvijas Banka has granted more than 20 fintech licences since January, as the country positions itself as a fast-track EU regulatory entry point. The post Latvia Issues 20-Plus Fintech Licences in 2026 as EU Gateway Push Grows appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Latvia’s financial regulator, Latvijas Banka, has issued more than 20 licences to fintech companies since the start of 2026, covering payment institutions, crowdfunding platforms, investment brokerages and crypto-asset service providers. The figures emerged at a workshop hosted in Riga by the FinTech Latvia Association (FLA) and the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), at which foreign representatives of the agency were briefed on the case for Latvia as an EU licensing base.

The event is part of a structured effort to channel inbound interest from fintech founders weighing up European domicile options. LIAA’s overseas representatives are frequently the first institutional point of contact for a foreign company exploring EU market entry, and the workshop aimed to equip them with a consistent, facts-based pitch.

The licensing proposition

Latvia’s central bank operates an Innovation Hub and a regulatory sandbox and offers free pre-licensing consultations. Latvijas Banka says a well-prepared application can be approved within two to three months of submission. That timeline, if borne out in practice, is notably compressed compared with some larger EU jurisdictions where authorisation processes can extend considerably longer and involve more procedural uncertainty.

Deputy Governor Santa Purgaile highlighted the country’s anti-money laundering record as a complementary asset. “Latvia was the first country assessed by MONEYVAL in its new, 6th evaluation round,” she noted, adding that the jurisdiction received a high or substantial effectiveness rating on ten of eleven outcomes. For compliance officers conducting jurisdictional due diligence, a strong MONEYVAL score carries material weight, particularly given the heightened scrutiny applied to Baltic financial centres in the years following a series of high-profile AML enforcement actions across the region.

Sector scale and strategic targets

Latvia’s licensed fintech base now stands at 127 companies. The sector employed 3,644 people at the end of 2024, a nine per cent increase year on year, and generated a total turnover of approximately €372 million. Profits reached €97 million, and the companies contributed more than €91 million in taxes, up 28 per cent on the prior year. Those unit economics give policymakers a clear fiscal argument for the sector’s expansion.

The cross-border reach is significant. More than 800,000 investors from outside Latvia invest through platforms licensed in the country, with German investors representing the largest single share. In aggregate, more than €13 billion has been deployed through Latvian-licensed investment platforms, which the FLA says account for close to a quarter of Europe’s peer-to-peer lending market by volume. The two largest fintech groups headquartered in Riga reported combined revenues exceeding €500 million in 2025, a figure larger than the entire domestic sector turnover, reflecting the degree to which Latvian licences are used as the legal anchor for pan-European and global operations.

Latvia’s Financial Technology Sector Development Strategy 2025 to 2027 targets a 30 per cent increase in the number of fintech companies, an 18 per cent rise in sector employment and a 15 per cent lift in attracted investment by the end of the period. FLA and LIAA will jointly attend Money20/20 Europe 2027 in Amsterdam and plan trade missions to Germany, Austria and France.

Competitive read-across

Latvia is competing for licensing mandates against a set of established EU alternatives. Lithuania built a similar proposition aggressively from 2016, becoming the dominant EU fintech licensing hub for firms exiting the UK after the Brexit referendum. Ireland and Luxembourg have captured asset management and payments mandates on the strength of their English-language environments and mature legal infrastructure. The Netherlands and Germany attract larger institutions. Latvia’s competitive angle rests on processing speed, regulator accessibility and AML credibility rather than market size or legal tradition. Whether that combination is sufficient to shift material deal flow away from Vilnius or Dublin will depend on whether the licensing timelines cited by Latvijas Banka hold at scale as application volumes increase. FLA plans to publish updated sector data in its annual Fintech Pulse 2026 report on 27 November.

title: M-Pesa at 20: Kenya’s Global Financial Inclusion Legacy
snippet: The following reflects on nearly 20 years of financial inclusion through Kenyan-born M-Pesa. The post M-Pesa at 20: Kenya’s Global Financial Inclusion Legacy appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The following reflects on nearly 20 years of financial inclusion through Kenyan-born M-Pesa.

When discussing the global fintech revolution, attention often turns to Silicon Valley, London or Singapore. Yet one of the most important financial innovations of the past two decades came from somewhere very different: Kenya.

In 2007, Safaricom launched M-Pesa, allowing people to send and receive money using a basic mobile phone. At the time, millions of Kenyans lacked access to traditional banking services, particularly those living outside major urban centres.

What followed was more than a technological innovation. M-Pesa fundamentally changed how ordinary people interacted with money.

Nearly 20 years later, its influence extends far beyond Kenya. From mobile payments in neighbouring African countries to digital wallets across Asia and other emerging markets, M-Pesa helped demonstrate that financial inclusion did not necessarily require a bank branch, a conventional bank account or even a smartphone.

Kenya’s transformation and Africa’s mobile money revolution

M-Pesa is everywhere in Kenya and has made its impact beyond just the country. Shown is in Nairobi, Kenya in October 20026 by Richie Santosdiaz

Before M-Pesa, transferring money between Nairobi and a rural community could involve travelling considerable distances, relying on informal arrangements or paying relatively expensive fees.

M-Pesa changed this by turning the mobile phone into a financial tool.

For many Kenyans, particularly those working in informal employment, small businesses and agriculture, this provided a practical way to participate in the financial system.

The impact has been significant. As highlighted in my earlier 2026 overview of Kenya’s fintech ecosystem for The Fintech Times, formal financial access has risen from approximately 26 per cent of adults in 2006 to around 85 per cent in recent years.

Whilst M-Pesa cannot claim sole responsibility, it has undoubtedly been central to this transformation.

It also helped establish Kenya as a leading African fintech hub, alongside Nigeria, South Africa and Egypt.

The wider significance is that Kenya demonstrated something other emerging economies could learn from: innovation does not always have to originate from the world’s wealthiest financial centres.

In fact, the absence of extensive traditional banking infrastructure helped create the conditions for a different approach.

Similar developments subsequently emerged elsewhere in Africa, including Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda and Senegal. As explored in my analysis of Senegal’s mobile money landscape, digital financial services are increasingly becoming an entry point into the formal economy.

In addition, M-Pesa can be argued has inspired innovation from beyond Africa such as in Southeast Asia with the likes of GCash in the Philippines for instance.

M-Pesa in 2026: Beyond sending and receiving money

The following was taken in October 2026 by Richie Santosdiaz in Nairobi, Kenya

Fast forward to 2026 and M-Pesa is no longer simply a money transfer service. It has developed into a broader financial ecosystem encompassing merchant payments, savings, credit, international transfers and services supporting businesses.

According to Safaricom’s financial year 2026 results, M-Pesa revenue increased by 13.4 per cent to KSh182.73billion, whilst its one-month active customer base reached approximately 41 million.

These figures illustrate how deeply the platform has become embedded in Kenya’s economy.

Perhaps more interesting is its expansion into Ethiopia, Africa’s second-most-populous country.

Safaricom Ethiopia reported that M-Pesa customers more than doubled to 5.2 million during its 2026 financial year. This expansion is important because Ethiopia has historically had a more restricted telecommunications and financial services environment.

Its experience could demonstrate how increased competition and digital financial infrastructure can accelerate financial inclusion in other markets.

However, challenges remain. Digital fraud, transaction costs, consumer protection and excessive borrowing through digital lending platforms raise legitimate concerns. Greater access to credit, for example, does not automatically translate into improved financial wellbeing.

Kenya’s own National Financial Inclusion Strategy 2025–2028 reflects the importance of developing a more inclusive and sustainable financial ecosystem.

The next chapter: From financial access to financial empowerment

Competition from the likes of Airtel is also making an impact across the African continent. Taken in October 2026 by Richie Santosdiaz in Nairobi, Kenya

The global opportunities for mobile money remain substantial. According to the GSMA‘s State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money 2026, there were 2.3 billion registered mobile money accounts worldwide last year, with transactions exceeding $2trillion.

However, only 593 million accounts were active within a 30-day period. This highlights an important distinction between financial access and meaningful financial participation.

The next phase of mobile money should therefore focus on three areas.

First, expanding access to savings, affordable credit and insurance, particularly for women, rural communities and small businesses.

Second, improving interoperability between banks, mobile wallets and international payment systems. For migrant workers sending remittances home, cheaper and faster cross-border payments could make a considerable difference.

Third, strengthening consumer protection and digital financial literacy. Financial inclusion means little if users cannot confidently and safely manage their money.

Artificial intelligence (AI) could also support more personalised financial services, although safeguards around data privacy and responsible lending will be essential.

Ultimately, M-Pesa’s greatest achievement is not simply the billions of dollars moving through its platform. It is that a solution developed around the everyday needs of Kenyans helped change how the world thinks about financial services.

As M-Pesa approaches its twentieth anniversary in 2027, the challenge is no longer proving that mobile money works. It is ensuring that the next generation of mobile money innovation helps people do more than transfer money: save, invest, build businesses and improve their economic prospects.

That would be an even greater legacy for an innovation that began in Kenya.

title: Butter Payments has been sold
snippet: The company was purchased last month, said its former chief executive, Charles Rosenblatt, who noted intensifying competitive pressures.
fullText:
Butter Payments, a business that has provided services to companies for managing customers’ subscription payments, has been acquired.

The company’s ex-CEO, Charles Rosenblatt, disclosed the sale in an interview last week. “We sold it about three weeks ago,” he said during a Friday interview. On his LinkedIn profile, Rosenblatt said the transaction took place in September.

He declined to name the company that has purchased Butter Payments, but said he expected the acquirer would make an announcement.

Butter Payments' business uses machine-learning algorithms and data from a consumer’s card and payment patterns to better understand why a subscription payment failed and how to resolve the problem. 

“Non-sufficient funds is usually the leading source, but another one of the big ones is suspected fraud,” Rosenblatt said in a February interview.

In a press release earlier this year, Butter Payments cited the churn added up to a collective $440 billion annually in lost revenue for companies with subscription payment methods.

During the interview last week, Rosenblatt explained how the payments business has changed so that services like those offered by Butter Payments have been absorbed into broader suites of services owned by larger companies, causing more competitive pressure from bigger players. It was “very tough as a monoline business,” he said. 

Rosenblatt likened the Butter Payments service to one of the myriad items listed on a restaurant’s menu. “What we built was better than anyone else, but for other companies, we were page 18 of a 20-page Cheesecake Factory menu,” Rosenblatt explained. “We were a better page 18. The problem is, what happens, competitively, is folks come in and offer page 18 for free, if you buy pages one through 17.” 

Digital payments juggernaut Stripe being one of those competitors was part of the problem. Rosenblatt shared how one client told him about the unbeatable offer that Stripe made.

“Stripe basically said to them, all the money they're saving you, we'll just pay you that in cash and take it off your bill to not do business with them and stay with us for everything,” Rosenblatt said. “It's hard to beat that, and that was millions of dollars.”

Facing that kind of competition would have required Butter Payments to raise more funds, so developing an exit plan became the more viable option, the ex-CEO said.

“We had a couple new products, but we … would have had to go raise a ridiculous amount of money to go expand,” Rosenblatt said. “Our investors, candidly, didn't have an appetite for that.”

As of February, the San Francisco-based business had raised nearly $40 million as of earlier this year. At its peak size, Butter Payments had about 53 employees.

Rosenblatt joined Butter Payments in June 2025 as its chief commercial officer, according to his LinkedIn profile. In November of last year, he was promoted to CEO, with marching orders to turn the business around after excessive spending, he said.

Prior to that role, he has been an adviser to investment companies and previously a payments consultant, but he had also held executive posts at companies including PayQuicker, Payoneer and Velo Payments, his LinkedIn profile showed.

Rosenblatt said he has counseled other companies with standalone approaches similar to the Butter Payments business to be aware of the encroaching competition.

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

title: AI’s real opportunity in payments is giving experts back their time
snippet: Advancing operational efficiency through intelligent guidance on errors and exception handling.

Picture a payments operator working through an exception queue. An item kicks out, and before it can be fixed, someone has to determine why: pull the transaction data, trace it through the relevant systems, check it against the rules of the network it is moving through and then decide on a corrective action. That kind of process plays out again and again across a bank's payment operations, every day, many times a day. Payment processing errors and exception handling remain both a heavy manual burden on operations teams and a detractor for overall end-customer experience, with disruptions costing the industry billions of dollars every year.

As payment volumes continue to rise, there is a big opportunity for banks to address this persistent pain point in payment operations and fuel growth. AI-driven automation that maintains human oversight offers a promising way to reimagine inefficient payment error and exception-handling processes by accelerating repairs, streamlining onboarding and improving the overall customer experience.

Accelerating repairs

Now consider that same operator working from a different starting point. AI has already surfaced the likely cause of the discrepancy, checked it against the applicable payment rules and recommended a fix. The operator reviews an assembled case, corrects it where needed and approves it, rather than building it from scratch. That is a faster task. Finastra’s data shows that this kind of guidance can reduce manual investigation time by 20-30%, saving payment operations teams more than 1.5 hours a day that would otherwise be spent diagnosing the same category of problem without this capability. That speed creates real operational capacity, enabling teams to handle more high-value customer experiences and create differentiation.

Enhancing operator onboarding

Payments infrastructure at most financial institutions is complex, built on years of integrations with institutional knowledge often concentrated among a handful of experienced staff. This makes learning a bank's payment systems no small task and places a premium on specialized skillsets. AI-powered automation capabilities targeted to support payment error reconciliation can shorten the learning curve by acting as a guide, helping new hires navigate the system and find the documentation or precedent they need. Just as important, it augments the specialized human expertise within organizations, since reliable repair guidance is now built into the workflow.

Becoming resilient and future proof

Payment rails are not static. Real-time schemes continue to roll out, ISO 20022 migration is reshaping message standards across markets, and cross-border corridors carry their own compliance requirements. A recommendation that is not validated against the current rules of the network a payment is moving through, such as SWIFT, Fedwire, SEPA, UPI or Nexus, cannot be trusted. Scheme-aware repair recommendations should identify discrepancies and underlying causes, delivering a proposed fix that is accurate and compliant with scheme and network requirements. With cloud-native infrastructure, AI-powered payments reconciliation recommender capabilities provide the flexibility to update rules without multi-year re-platforming whenever a standard changes. That combination is what resilience means in payment operations: staying accurate and compliant as the rules governing payments continue to change.

Modernization and AI readiness are becoming less of an efficiency upgrade and more of a growth requirement. The time, manual effort and specialized expertise required to keep error and exception-handling operations running smoothly have, for years, limited how quickly banks can scale. Solving that back-office barrier is part of what will separate the institutions that grow from those that do not.

title: Financial Solutions Adds AI and Compliance Checks to Wealth Pilot
snippet: The Exeter IFA network has upgraded its adviser portal with automated file checking and an FCA-fluent AI assistant, both operating on a single centralised The post Financial Solutions Adds AI and Compliance Checks to Wealth Pilot appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Financial Solutions has launched an upgraded version of Wealth Pilot, its adviser workspace platform, bringing automated compliance file checks and an AI assistant onto a single client record. The Exeter-based IFA network said the update, released on 12 October 2026, is designed to eliminate the data re-keying and siloed systems that advisers commonly encounter when using separate compliance and AI tools.

Wealth Pilot was first introduced in January 2025 as a client onboarding and servicing portal built on Microsoft‘s Power Platform. The latest iteration consolidates fact finds, risk profiles, financial plans, cashflow data and client documents into one unified record, with compliance and AI tooling operating directly on that record rather than on exported copies.

The key product additions

Leanne Williams, managing director of Financial Solutions

Two features sit at the centre of the upgrade. The first, Case Checks, applies a rule-based compliance review to every advice file before sign-off, rather than sampling a subset. Files receive Green, Amber or Red ratings, each accompanied by the underlying evidence and a list of required remediation steps. Where the system cannot confirm a finding, it defaults to Amber for manual review. Reports are produced in Word and Excel format and include references to the relevant FCA Handbook provisions.

The second addition, Adviser Intelligence, is an AI assistant that answers case-level queries using the firm’s own records and the adviser’s role permissions. It surfaces direct links to the FCA Handbook, flags data inconsistencies in real time and drafts suitability reports in the firm’s own template. Crucially, all AI-generated content requires adviser approval before it reaches the client record or any client-facing output.

Leanne Williams, managing director of Financial Solutions, framed the design philosophy around auditability. “An AI tool that cannot show its working is not much use to a compliance officer,” she said. “Every Case Checks rating comes from a written rule, every finding comes with its evidence, and if the system is not sure, a person looks at it.”

Data control is a deliberate commercial and compliance choice. Financial Solutions hosts the platform within its own Microsoft environment, meaning client data is not used to train AI models and the firm retains direct control over fields, forms and dashboards without depending on a third-party vendor’s release schedule. Access is governed by Microsoft sign-in and role-based permissions, with a full audit trail ensuring each member firm on the network sees only its own clients.

Market context and regulatory read-across

The product sits squarely in the expanding market for compliance-adjacent regtech tooling aimed at wealth management intermediaries. The FCA’s Consumer Duty rules, which came into full force in July 2023 for new business and July 2024 for closed books, have raised the evidentiary standard advisers must meet when demonstrating suitability and client understanding. Vulnerability assessment and outcome monitoring, both featured in Wealth Pilot’s workflow, are areas where the regulator has signalled continued supervisory attention.

The broader competitive landscape for adviser technology includes established platform providers, compliance software vendors and a growing number of AI-native tools targeting the suitability report and file-review workflow. Financial Solutions’ differentiation claim rests on vertical integration: by owning the data model rather than connecting to third-party systems via API, it argues that compliance tooling and AI can operate with greater accuracy and auditability than bolt-on solutions. Whether that closed-architecture approach proves an advantage or a constraint as the AI layer matures will depend heavily on how quickly the firm can iterate on the underlying model.

Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: Money20/20 USA day one: Las Vegas asks who is holding the bag
snippet: Day one in Las Vegas on the stablecoin and agent stages. Every panel I sat in kept circling one question: when money moves itself, who carries the risk? The post Money20/20 USA day one: Las Vegas asks who is holding the bag appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Day one in Las Vegas on the stablecoin and agent stages. Every panel I sat in kept circling one question: when money moves itself, who carries the risk?

I spent Monday, the first full day of Money20/20 USA at The Venetian, moving between the Meridian and Intersection stages with a recorder running. By the afternoon I could have written the same sentence under every session. Nobody I heard was still arguing about whether stablecoins or AI agents work. The argument was about who carries the risk when they do something nobody intended.

Trust before scale

It started with Mastercard. Just before its late-morning stablecoin panel, Ann Johnson, who runs security solutions at Mastercard, launched Stablecoin Security, a risk score for stablecoin payments that combines 16 years of the network’s fraud, identity and cyber intelligence with blockchain analytics and is built to work at machine speed. Her framing was simple: “the thing that allows innovation to scale is trust.” Mastercard says it will launch in North America first, with worldwide availability expected in 2027.

The panel that followed made the case for why it is needed. Rajpal Khangura, co-founder and chief compliance officer of Keyrails, settles trade payments for merchants in markets such as Nigeria paying suppliers in China, with an average ticket of $250,000 to $350,000. His customers used to ask only how cheap and how fast; now they ask how safe the wallet is, and how safe the fiat is when it lands. His hardest problem is the wallet that is not sanctioned itself but has transacted a few hops away from one that is, and keeping his own risk appetite in step with every bank and liquidity partner downstream. He also told the room it can still be quicker to put cash in the back of a van and drive it across a border than to send the payment.

Keith Vander Leest, who runs BVNK in the US and is now part of Mastercard, said too much stablecoin activity is still trading and he wants real-world payments to become the majority. That, in his view, depends on building quickly the protections the fiat world took decades to build, and on carrying far more data with each payment on chain, from ISO 20022 messages to travel rule information. Alex Garn of Borderless said the US can learn from instant payments in the UK, where extra checks happen at the moment a new payee is added, and from Pix in Brazil, where fraud is fought by sharing signals across the whole network rather than bank by bank. His one-word answer to what the industry must get right was invisible.

The enterprise view

Earlier that morning, on the Intersection Stage, Nik Milanović of This Week in Fintech chaired From Pilot to Payout, a panel with Payoneer, eBay and Citi. He opened with Payoneer’s new survey of 265 payments, treasury and finance leaders, in which 69 per cent are already using stablecoins and 41 per cent at meaningful scale, then asked the room who had actually paid with one. I counted six or seven hands, in a room full of payments professionals.

The panel explained the gap. Renata Camera Santos, head of wallet at eBay, said a marketplace has to give buyers and sellers the same experience whatever the rail, and that solving for the happy path is not enough when card payments have had decades to work through every edge case. Every vendor pitches stablecoins as if the world is your oyster, Santos said, when what a marketplace needs is to be told where the oyster is. Pix in Brazil, where Santos grew up, already delivers much of what stablecoins promise, so a stablecoin has to fix a margin or speed problem better than that.

Will Artingstall, Citi’s head of banking as a service, said that for the first time a new-product conversation with clients was about risk rather than features, with a new vocabulary of know-your-transaction checks and hosted and unhosted wallets, and that the dispute rights a card holder takes for granted have no stablecoin equivalent yet. Where Citi has seen strong take-up is tokenised deposits, because clients fund from an ordinary account and never hold a wallet while the token is minted and burned behind the scenes. Rowland Berry of Payoneer added that however much of the stack you outsource, the accountability stays with whoever holds the licence.

Agents need papers

The afternoon session on the trust layer for agentic commerce, with Mastercard, Skyfire and Forter, was the most useful half hour of my day. Ranjita Iyer, executive vice president of services for North America at Mastercard, chaired it and said the network expects one transaction in ten could be made by an agent by 2030, possibly sooner. Adam Davies, director of AI strategy at Forter, set out what a merchant now has to establish for every agent at the door: which person it represents, whether it is acting within the authority it was given, and what credential it is paying with. Each already has rival standards, from Visa‘s Trusted Agent Protocol and Google’s AP2 to Mastercard’s Verifiable Intent and Stripe‘s shared payment tokens, and no merchant can realistically support them all alone.

Amir Sarhangi of Skyfire said we built the internet for humans and today’s fraud tools are probabilistic, while merchants now want to know with certainty which agents are good and who is behind them. Skyfire’s Know Your Agent token binds a verified business behind an agent to verified details of its user, and Forter reads it at checkout. Merchants, he said, do not want a separate registration for agents; they want the agent recognised as the customer it acts for, loyalty account and all.

Then Iyer raised the question that has followed this whole autumn of conferences. When an agent buys something its owner did not authorise, or simply gets it wrong, the issuer needs that identity and intent data to deal with the liability and, in Iyer’s words, “to figure out who’s holding the bag on those types of transactions.”

Rules after innovation

I finished on the Intersection Stage with former CFTC Chairman J. Christopher Giancarlo, a month after the CLARITY Act failed a Senate procedural vote. He was relaxed about it. “As someone who wrote rules at the CFTC, I’m not that disappointed that clarity didn’t get done,” he said, arguing that the US should let innovation solve commercial problems first and legislate once the public policy issues are clear, as his old agency is now doing with prediction markets. He predicted that by 2040 anything of value that can be tokenised will be.

Karin Kusano, the crypto strategist known as Cryptomommi, gave the session its human side, describing how ordinary banking shut her out when she had no fixed address. She then turned on her own industry: crypto has behaved like a teenager, she said, and needs to grow up, starting with pump-and-dump schemes and meme coins.

Around the floor

Elsewhere on Monday, Huntington launched The 1866 Studio, an agentic small business platform built with Google Cloud, Proof and Circle demonstrated an agent proving who it acts for and then paying in USDC, and Skyfire and Forter formalised the partnership discussed on stage. Day two brings FDIC Chairman Travis Hill in conversation with the Financial Technology Association at 10:00 Pacific time.

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

  

            						

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 28 September 2026, Raymondip Bedi was ordered to pay £603,404.28 and Patrick Mavanga £247,997.99.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

Notes to editors

Raymondip Bedi’s date of birth is 9 October 1989.

Patrick Mavanga’s date of birth is 24 November 1984.

FCA secures convictions against two individuals for £1.5m fraud.

Two individuals sentenced to a combined 12 years for £1.5m crypto fraud.

Confiscation orders are made under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and require offenders to repay the benefit they gained from criminal conduct or the value of their available assets, whichever is lower.

If the defendants fail to pay the confiscation orders within 3 months, Bedi will face up to an additional 5 years in prison and Mavanga could face up to 2 years.

The FCA has previously sought to contact affected investors. Anyone who believes they may have been affected and has not heard from the FCA should contact the FCA's Consumer Helpline.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5 year strategy.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more information about the FCA.

title: TransBridge Advisors Flags Five US Licensing Traps for Fintechs
snippet: US regulatory adviser TransBridge Advisors has set out five licensing missteps that can stall international fintechs before they launch in the American market. The post TransBridge Advisors Flags Five US Licensing Traps for Fintechs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TransBridge Advisors, a US-focused fintech regulatory consultancy, has published an advisory piece identifying five licensing errors it says consistently delay or derail international fintechs attempting to enter the American market. The firm says the problems tend to originate well before a regulator ever reviews an application.

The core argument is structural: the US is a fragmented regulatory environment in which the same product can generate different obligations depending on how funds move, which entities hold them, and where customers are physically located. A business holding a single national licence elsewhere may need federal compliance, state authorisations, banking arrangements, and ongoing maintenance obligations in the US, each with its own cost and sequencing dependency.

The five failure modes

TransBridge identifies FinCEN registration as the most common source of confusion. Registration as a Money Services Business under the Bank Secrecy Act establishes federal anti-money laundering obligations, but it is not a nationwide money transmission licence. Whether a company also needs state-level money transmitter authorisations depends on the activities performed, the operating structure, and the laws of each relevant jurisdiction. That distinction, the firm says, typically surfaces late, during bank onboarding or investor due diligence, rather than at the design stage.

The second error is building a product architecture before assessing its regulatory perimeter. A cross-border payments platform and a software provider to a licensed institution may appear similar to the customer but face materially different licensing analysis. The same product combined with stablecoin settlement or digital asset custody could trigger an additional set of requirements. TransBridge argues that commissioning a regulatory perimeter assessment while the operating model is still flexible is considerably cheaper than renegotiating commercial agreements or redesigning transaction flows after they are in place.

Third, the firm warns that the cost of a multi-state licensing programme is routinely underestimated. Filing fees are visible; the management time, surety bond obligations, minimum net worth requirements, compliance system builds, and extended regulatory correspondence are less so. For a venture-backed company, a licensing exercise that overruns its timetable can affect runway and the assumptions underpinning the next funding round.

The fourth error is filing broadly rather than building a jurisdiction-specific strategy. TransBridge suggests mapping the licensing programme back to the commercial rollout: which customers will be served first, where regulated activity will take place, and which authorisations must be in hand before revenue can be generated. The note also flags acquisition of a licensed entity as an option that requires its own analysis, since change-of-control approvals, historical compliance obligations, and operational integration can introduce as much work as building the portfolio directly.

Fifth, the firm addresses post-licence compliance. Holding a state licence does not guarantee banking access, and the compliance framework in place at initial authorisation may not be adequate for a business two years into operation with a larger customer base and higher transaction volumes.

Regulatory context

The advisory carries particular relevance given the current US legislative environment. TransBridge specifically notes the GENIUS Act, the federal stablecoin framework that is now in force, and flags that operators issuing, distributing, or building services around payment stablecoins face an additional compliance layer sitting alongside state money transmission laws. The Act introduces requirements for reserve composition, redemption rights, and AML obligations that interact with existing state frameworks in ways that have not yet been fully resolved through rulemaking.

For international operators, the broader picture is one of convergence pressure. The EU’s PSD3 and MiCA frameworks are pushing towards a more centralised licensing model for payments and digital assets respectively, a direction that contrasts sharply with the US state-by-state architecture. Fintechs scaling across both regulatory environments need to treat them as structurally distinct problems rather than variations on the same theme.

TransBridge is promoting a 30-minute licensing assessment alongside the piece and has made a US Fintech Licensing Roadmap and a GENIUS Act Compliance Checklist available for download. The firm is not a law firm, and the publication carries a disclaimer that it does not constitute legal or regulatory advice.
